doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: French jazz musicians and American influence
summary: Do French players still aspire to sound American? He says the younger generation writes original, ECM-like music.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I want to read, this is connected to jazz in Europe. And it had an interview with Pierre Boussaguet and —

He said this about American jazz. He says — he was talking about playing with visiting jazz musicians. “It’s an honor because jazz to me has always been, historically speaking, a pure American art form that’s so powerful, so joyful that it spread throughout the world.” And another quote from the pianist Rossano Sportiello from Italy, who now lives here. He said, “The most beautiful compliment that we could tell each other was, ‘Tonight you sounded like an American’.” So my question is nowadays do jazz musicians in France still aspire to sound like Americans or have they developed their own personality?

I think it’s more the latter than the former. You know I don’t know exactly like, the time period-wise, like when the university, the conservatory system started here with jazz departments, like I think maybe earlier in the States than it has over here. But like the main conservatory here in Paris, there are a lot of great young musicians and they’re definitely into, I don’t want to say avante garde, because it’s not just that, but it’s more about writing their own original music that has kind of like an ECM kind of European quality. They’re not really playing bebop although teachers are teaching that as something you have to have but that’s not the end, it’s just kind of a means to an end. So I would say yes, it’s definitely less about emulation and sounding American except they’re obviously influenced by, you know a lot of the young piano players I think as opposed to maybe sounding like Wynton Kelly, they’re into Brad Mehldau. Right? Which I guess that’s kind of a natural generational thing, although we’re also telling these young guys before you go to Brad you have to check out Wynton, because Brad checked out Wynton. You know so it’s like the whole lineage part of developing. But definitely the younger generation, they’re more into the odd meter kind of thing, blending Afro — or ethnic kind of world music stuff, Steve Coleman kind of influence, Robert
Glasper. You know so there’s more of that going on. So maybe influence by American musicians but a different generation of them.
